title: Thangka painting
hook: painted scrolls made by exact rules, used in meditation

segments.voice: Yesterday, Milarepa's songs, sung to a deer, a dog and a furious hunter. Your line was sing it. Did that one line come back while you cooked or walked? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

A painter sits on a cushion with a stretched piece of cotton propped in front of her. She hasn't drawn a single face yet. Instead, with a ruler and a fine charcoal line, she is drawing a grid: a center line, cross lines, careful measured marks, like a builder laying out a house. Only when the grid is right does the figure begin: the head here, the heart there, the hands exactly so many units from the center. It will take a long time. The finished painting can be rolled up and carried on a horse. It's a thangka.
screen: `A GRID BEFORE A FACE.` → `HEAD HERE, HEART THERE.` → `ROLLED UP, CARRIED ON A HORSE.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. A thangka is a Tibetan painted scroll, usually on cotton, framed in silk brocade and fitted with a rod so it can be rolled up. It could travel with a teacher or a nomad family and be hung wherever the practice happened that day. Some monasteries keep giant thangkas that are unrolled across a hillside on festival days. Second, the rules. Thangka painters learn measurement systems handed down in texts and from master to student. Each kind of figure has its proportions: a peaceful buddha one set, a wrathful protector another. A painter isn't free to stretch a face or shrink a hand for effect. The rules carry the teaching, so that a figure painted today matches the figure described long ago. Third, the making. The colors are traditionally ground from minerals and plants, sometimes with gold. Painters train for years under a teacher. Tradition says the eyes are often painted last, and then a lama consecrates the painting, and it is understood to be more than a picture: a support for the presence of what it shows. Fourth, the use. A thangka is made to be looked at in meditation. A practitioner gazes at the figure, every detail, the hands, the colors, the ornaments, then closes the eyes and builds it again in the mind. Here the exact rules matter most. A face drawn by whim would be a different face each time. A face painted by rule can be held steady, by many people, across generations.
screen: `A SCROLL THAT ROLLS AND TRAVELS.` · `PROPORTIONS HANDED DOWN.` · `MINERAL COLORS, EYES LAST.` · `GAZE, CLOSE THE EYES, REBUILD.` · then, large: `PAINTED BY RULE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look closely at one painting. It can be a thangka found online, a print on your wall, a photo you love. Settle, and let your eyes rest on it. Take in the whole thing first. Then go detail by detail: a hand, a color, an edge, a small thing in a corner you never noticed. Go slowly. When you feel you've really seen it, close your eyes and try to see it again, as clearly as you can. Open them and look at what you missed. The bell holds the time.
Thangka. A Tibetan painted scroll, made to exact proportions with mineral colors, and used as a support for meditation. Today's word.
Your line: painted by rule. Today, do one small task by a careful rule, folding, writing, tidying, and see what the care does to your attention. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists hang thangkas in homes, temples and retreat rooms; trained painters make them to set proportions, a lama consecrates them, and practitioners gaze at them to support visualization in meditation.
